rv.q: Bean and Chris's dialogue is a joyous blizzard of bawdy Carry-On innuendo, rolled out at such a torrential rate that it's borderline genius or gibberish — but either way splendidly sends up political correctness and verbal prudery in general.
It is all, in its irrepressible, rambunctious way, every bit as clever as it is deliciously daft. You can't help but surrender to it.
This knowing mix of satire, filth, clowning, pastiche, wartime derring-do and romance absolutely hit my sweet spot.
The National has a summer hit on its hands.
But when it doubles down on being a silly, rollicking, escapist comedy, it's the giddiest night of theatre you'll have all summer.
It's always relatively entertaining, often very funny indeed, but its frothiness becomes tiresome after a while and it's more celebratory than interrogative of the time it's portraying.
Still, in director Emily Burns's hands, this play isn't dizzyingly funny in the way that One Man, Two Guvnors so often was, perhaps because of its lack of physical comedy.

The script has a self-consciously Boy’s Own ‘whizzo’ feel and drips with arch knowingness and nods to its own theatricality, which is amusing enough but prevents us from caring much about what happens to anyone.
It's funny. It's fine. We all need a chuckle at the moment. But 'Jack Again' isn't anything more than the sum of its laughs.
For me, at almost three hours on its final preview night, this comedy felt forced, unoriginal and drawn out.
This vast space isn't really suited to drama at all... and yet this ravishing and hilarious show fits the sprawling emptiness perfectly.
Comedy lighting does strike twice. As the ultra-British 1940s types peopling the farcical plot might put it, 'Hurrah!'
It looks like with Jack Again, he may have done it again.

The performances are uniformly (no pun intended) superb, and the company have an infectious joie-de-vivre. ... Although the pandemic delayed its premiere, 'Jack Again' proves the perfect tonic to the miserable few years we have been through.
The result is a play which frequently, rightly, brings the house down. Again may not be perfect, it is still incredibly enjoyable.

Mark Thompson’s design illustrates the production’s sweet spot: a technicolour combination of comic book and live action, Englishness as an aesthetic and a myth. 'Jack Absolute' is more content to cuddle up to that myth than to seriously challenge it, but as pure summer fizz, it goes down a treat.
Jack Again does settle into a veritable hoot. With a skilled and hugely likeable cast, it's genuinely funny and charming, spectacularly, beautifully staged, and ultimately quite moving.
Jack Again isn't an attempt to show the relevance of an eighteenth century play to our own time but a new confection, a crowd-pleaser with an eye on the box office.

All these ingredients combine to serve an affectionate lampooning of wartime Englishness. Set in 1940 against a backdrop of West Sussex rolling hills, the cherry on designer Mark Thompson’s chocolate box set is a Hurricane fighter plane suspended over Mrs Malaprop’s mansion which has been requisitioned by the RAF.
This is a comedy that's definitely worth seeing, even if it could have benefited from a little streamlining.
